hook: The extension that got backdoored was the official one, from the verified account.
angle: Most developer-tooling policies are written to stop typosquats and rogue forks. This incident inverted that assumption: the malicious build shipped through the vendor's own verified marketplace account, which makes extension auto-update an unreviewed code path into machines that hold cloud CLI sessions. Walk through the three controls that actually change the blast radius — short-lived federated credentials on developer workstations instead of long-lived keys, inventory you can query by package and version, and a documented answer to 'which machines installed version X between A and B'. Advisory framing, no vendor blame, concrete checks a reader can run this week.

hook: Your eval harness told the agent it was a test before it read a single instruction.
angle: Two Microsoft posts in two weeks point the same direction: change the environment under test and the behaviour changes. A local git remote made the agent 11 percentage points less likely to push on its own; a workspace folder literally named like an eval tells the agent it is being graded. The lesson for anyone signing off on agent evaluations is that harness details are experimental variables, so neutral workspace names, a harness review step, and re-baselining after any cost optimisation belong in the method rather than a footnote.

hook: When an auditor asks who touched the HSM, platform logs are not the strongest answer.
angle: Azure Cloud HSM now emits audit records generated by the device itself, covering authentication, administrator changes, policy updates, key lifecycle, and backup and restore. That is evidence from inside the cryptographic boundary rather than from the control plane describing it. Frame it as an evidence-chain design exercise for regulated workloads: what counts as audit-relevant, where the log lands, how long it is retained immutably, and how it correlates with the control-plane trail you already keep.

hook: A pipeline can be 99th-percentile fast and still report the wrong number.
angle: Two data stories this week belong in the same conversation. Multi-table ACID transactions on Unity Catalog remove the main reason to keep a relational tier in front of the lakehouse, and event-time watermarks decide whether the aggregates landing in it are actually complete. For clinical or financial reporting the second one is the risk: latency dashboards stay green while correctness quietly drifts. Argue for lateness as a documented business decision, a stated fate for late events, and a monitor on event-time lag that is separate from processing lag.

hook: Agents are going to call your APIs. The time to decide the contract was last year.
angle: Consumer agents browsing, booking, and transacting on someone's behalf have crossed from demo to default, and computer-use models widen what an agent can touch from 'our APIs' to 'any interface we can log into'. The architect's move is unglamorous and urgent: classify which services a non-human principal may call, define the scoped token and delegated-consent model, set rate and spend ceilings, and make sure every agent action leaves an audit record you can reconstruct. If you cannot answer 'which agent did this, on whose behalf, with what permission' today, that is the gap to close.
